```text
Either recurrence costs O(1) per coefficient. Both are synthetic division of G by a linear factor,
that is, polynomial deflation, which is unstable in general; Knyazev and Oosterhuis [18] mention
Equation (14) but set it aside for that reason. The classical analysis of Peters and Wilkinson [27]
shows that deflation is stable if it starts from the constant term when the removed root is large
in modulus, and from the leading coefficient when it is small. The roots of G are the negative
reals −1/αj , so here the two regimes are separated by a single threshold, |−1/αi | ≥ 1 if and only if
qi ≥ 1/2, and the direction alone controls the error.
```

```text
Implementation. The inner loops of Algorithm 1 run over players for a fixed place, so the
placement matrix is stored place-major, and the players of a direction group, which are contiguous
after sorting, are processed in blocks. The recurrences of different players are independent, so the
loops vectorize. The 2n evaluations of exp and expm1 are the only transcendental operations at a
node. Each node adds its contribution to all nm entries of the matrix, so the nodes are processed in
blocks of 32, which streams the matrix through memory once per block instead of once per node.
The nodes are independent, so the outer loop parallelizes across threads; a fixed assignment of nodes
to threads and a fixed reduction order keep the result bit-for-bit reproducible.
```

```text
5       Numerical results
All results come from a stand-alone implementation of Algorithm 1 written for this paper, run on
the grid of Section 3.3 unless a sweep varies it, on an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D (16 cores) under
WSL2 with GCC 14.2 at -O3 -march=native.

5.1     Validation suite and accuracy
Claims at the level of 10−14 cannot be checked by Monte Carlo, whose standard error decreases as
the inverse square root of the number of samples, nor by general-purpose exact evaluation, which
is infeasible beyond about 30 players. The suite therefore consists of instances whose placement
probabilities or equities have closed forms or low-dimensional exact dynamic programs that scale
to n = 4,000 (Section D): winner-take-all, two-prize, flat and linear prize structures on arbitrary
stacks, and arbitrary prize structures on equal stacks, on two stack sizes, on equal stacks with
up to ten exceptions, and on small fields with n ≤ 20. The stacks range from equal to geometric
progressions, Zipf and log-normal draws and single outliers, with ratios up to ρ = 109 ; the prizes
range from winner-take-all to flat, linear, top-heavy and realistic payouts and to satellites paying
the top half, the top 80% or all but the last player (Section E). The references are evaluated in
double-double arithmetic, so their own rounding error is far below the errors measured. The suite
has 1,511 instances with n from 3 to 4,000, formed from 189 stack vectors and 10 prize structures;
141 of them have multiple references and are checked against each, 1,662 comparisons in all.
    Table 3 gives the worst errors by field size. Every field size is at the rounding floor of Remark 3.3:
over all instances the worst relative error of an equity is 4.0 × 10−14 and the worst absolute error of
a placement probability 1.1 × 10−14 , with 250 nodes up to 30 players and 2,000 up to 4,000. The
row and column sums of the matrix, accumulated in double-double arithmetic, deviate from one by
at most 2.2 × 10−14 and 4.7 × 10−13 ; the column sums grow faster with n because in fields with large
groups of equal stacks thousands of identical rounding errors add coherently. For the families with
                                                                                P

combination of them, Vi = r (πr − πr+1 )Fi,r , so this figure bounds the relative error of the equities
```

```text
    The sweeps and comparisons below run on a smaller extremal set of 25 instances per field
size, chosen from the error budget: groups of equal stacks, which minimize the estimated width
(Lemma 3.2), with the prize structures that expose the deep places, and fields spanning the full
ratio ρ, for which the truncation bounds are tight. To check that it captures the largest errors of
the validation suite, we run the whole suite at twice the step of Section 3.3, where the worst errors
are above the floor: they agree with those of the extremal set exactly for probabilities and to within
0.2% for equities (Section E).

5.2                                    Quadrature rules
Figure 2 compares the exp-exp lattice with the quadrature rules of MPL and LAQI, in the same
leave-one-out engine and on the extremal set with n ≤ 1,000. The MPL rule is Gauss–Legendre
in the Gumbel variable on a window set from the range of the scores with a quantile margin l; it
is shown with its published margin l = 10−5 and with l = 10−18 , which makes the omitted tails
negligible at the target accuracy. The LAQI rule is composite Gauss–Legendre in log(1 + t) on 32
panels with the breaks set from the instance. The engine integrates every place, including the first,
and applies no output rescaling; in the published implementations, MPL evaluates the first place
analytically and LAQI rescales its equities to the prize pool.
    At its published margin the MPL rule levels off at an absolute error of 10−5 in the probabilities
and a relative error of order n l in the equities. Once truncation is negligible, the rules differ only
in how their nodes are spread over log t. The exp-exp lattice reaches the floor at 1,000 nodes for
both quantities. Before the floor, the LAQI rule is more accurate than the lattice for equities
and less accurate for probabilities; it reaches the floor at 1,024 nodes for equities and at 1,536 for
probabilities. With its breaks fixed for the stack-ratio bound instead of set from the instance, it
needs 1,536 nodes for both quantities in our implementation (not shown). The MPL rule with the
wide margin needs 2,260 and 3,200. The per-node cost of Algorithm 1 does not depend on the rule,
so at a given accuracy the order of the curves is also the order of the running times.
```

```text
5.3    Leave-one-out schemes
Table 4 runs Algorithm 1 with its leave-one-out step replaced: each single-direction recurrence alone,
the direction rule of Section 4.2 with and without the clamp, and the prefix–suffix products of
Knyazev and Oosterhuis [18]. Neither single direction is usable: each overflows on some instances,
and even with the clamp it loses every digit on others. The direction rule alone brings the equity
error down to the level of the residue described in Section 4.2, and the clamp removes it. The
prefix–suffix products agree with the clamped deconvolution to the rounding floor on equities and on
absolute probability errors, and they keep relative accuracy on small probabilities; on the instances
their row covers, they take about 27 times the total running time.

5.4    Runtime
Table 5 reports the wall-clock time of Algorithm 1 on one thread and on eight. The single-thread
time grows as n2 per node, as the cost analysis of Section 4.3 predicts, and the number of nodes
grows as n1/2 , in powers of two: the step halves between n = 1,000 and n = 2,000, which adds a
factor of two, while n = 2,000 and n = 4,000 share a step. Eight threads give a speed-up of 4.8
to 6.0 for n ≥ 1,000. For comparison, our Monte Carlo implementation at n = 4,000 takes 167
microseconds per sampled finishing order. Estimating a probability of 10−3 with a relative standard
error of 10−3 would require about 109 samples, resulting in about two CPU-days. MPL reports
about 2 ms per query for K = 10 places with 200 nodes on a GPU in single precision [18], and LAQI
2.47 s for the equities of 4,000 players with 192 nodes in Node.js [32]; implementations, outputs and
accuracies differ, so these figures are not directly comparable with ours.
```

```text
6     Related work
6.1   Self-organizing lists and caching
The move-to-front (MTF) rule maintains a list of n records; a requested record, drawn with
probability pi independently of the past, is moved to the front. The stationary distribution of
the resulting chain on permutations is the Plackett–Luce distribution [12], so the stationary MTF
list is an ICM finishing order with pi = si /S, and the depth of a record, its search cost, is its
place minus one. Two performance measures of self-organizing search are special cases of the ICM.
With linear prizes, the equity is an affine function of the expected search cost, whose average over
requests McCabe [23] gave in closed form. With unit prizes for the top C places, it is the item’s hit
probability of a least-recently-used (LRU) cache of capacity C.
    The distribution of the search cost was first derived by Burville and Kingman [4], as an alternating
sum over subsets of records. The integral representation appeared in two steps. Flajolet et al. [9]
obtained, by formal-language methods, an integral form for the search-cost distribution and the LRU
fault probability, and proposed evaluating it by numerical integration. Fill and Holst [8] rederived
it by embedding the chain in Poisson time, where the search cost of a record, conditioned on its
exponential age, is Poisson-binomial. Their Theorem 1 divides the full product by one record’s factor
inside the integral, which is the leave-one-out operation of Section 4.2 at the level of generating
functions; Theorem 2.2 is its per-record statement. The representation has since served exact and
asymptotic analyses of MTF and LRU [7, 16, 20], always for aggregate quantities; none of the works
cited here computes the placement distributions of all records to a controlled accuracy.

6.2   Poisson-binomial computation and quadrature
At a fixed node the coefficients Cr form a Poisson-binomial distribution; Hong [15] and Biscarri et al.
[1] survey the methods for computing it. Leave-one-out quantities arise in conditional Bernoulli
sampling, where Chen and Liu [5] compute them for all elements through power sums. The direction
rule of Theorem 4.1 is classical in polynomial deflation [27] but, to our knowledge, has not been
recorded for this distribution. Double-exponential transformations [25, 30, 31] are usually applied
adaptively to one integral at a time; here the step and the window are fixed once for a class of
inputs, and Section 5.2 compares the resulting lattice with Gauss rules as a node layout.

6.3   Plackett–Luce rank marginals and the ICM in practice
Placement probabilities of Plackett–Luce policies serve as propensities in off-policy evaluation and
determine exposures in fair ranking [26], and they have been estimated by sampling rankings [3, 19].
Knyazev and Oosterhuis [18] (MPL) compute them by numerical integration of the Poisson-binomial
representation, derived from the Gumbel formulation, for the top K places, with K ≤ 30 in their
experiments. The window of their Gauss–Legendre rule is set from the range of the scores and
grows with their spread. They set the division recurrence aside because avoiding division “leads to
high numerical stability,” and measure accuracy against a 107 -sample Monte Carlo oracle. Table 6
sets their design and that of LAQI against DE-ICM, and Section 5.2 measures both quadrature
rules under our stack-ratio bound.
    For the ICM itself, exact calculators stop at a few dozen players, Monte Carlo simulation
[29] is the reference for validation, and commercial tools use undisclosed approximations [14]. In
game-theoretic analyses of tournament play, the payoff of a hand is the value of the resulting stacks:
Miltersen and Sørensen [24] compute it by solving the recursive game, as the probability of winning
```

```text
the heads-up tournament, and Ganzfried and Sandholm [10] start from the ICM and refine it by
iteration. The ICM itself has been examined as a model by Diaconis and Ethier [6] and Kim [17].
    Wolters [32] (LAQI) published a deterministic method on the same representation, which was
reached through the storage-and-search connection mentioned in the GTO Wizard post [2]. It returns
equities only, and its comparison with exact values covers fields of up to 13 players; larger fields
are checked by self-convergence and against Monte Carlo. Its adjoint pass obtains all equities from
forward prefix states at O(nm) per node, and on the exp-exp grid it can replace the deconvolution of
Section 4 when only equities are needed. A fixed grid also permits reuse of intermediate quantities,
including adjoint states, that depend only on stacks and prizes unchanged between instances,
provided the instances use a common normalization scale and satisfy the bounds used to choose the
grid.


7     Discussion and conclusion
DE-ICM computes the placement marginals of any Plackett–Luce distribution given as positive
weights, within the stack-ratio bound its grid was set for. It therefore applies directly to the
propensities and exposures of Section 6.3, where the weights are exponentiated scores, and to the
depth distributions of records under the move-to-front rule and the hit probabilities of items in LRU
caches, which are rows or partial sums of the same matrix. Its per-node cost is O(n2 ) regardless
of the number of places requested; when only a few places or only the equities are needed, the
prefix–suffix products or the adjoint pass have lower asymptotic cost on the same grid (Section 4.3).
    Two limitations remain. Probabilities that are themselves small are accurate in absolute but
not in relative terms; where relative accuracy is required in the tails, the prefix–suffix products can
replace the deconvolution for the places concerned, at a cost that grows quadratically in the number
of places (Section 5.3). And the ICM is a model, whose adequacy is a separate question [17].

Reproducibility. Algorithm 1 with the grid of Section 3.3 and Section C specifies the method,
and Sections D and E the reference families and the validation suite. This description is intended to
support independent reimplementation and comparison against the same reference families. The
implementation used in the paper is independent of the production code; neither is released.
```

```text
Conclusion. The placement probabilities of the ICM, and of any Plackett–Luce distribution,
can be computed for all players and all places at once, for fields of thousands of players, to nearly
the accuracy of double-precision arithmetic. Two pieces of numerical design make this possible on
top of a classical integral representation. The first is a double-exponential grid fixed once for the
admissible inputs, whose truncation errors are bounded in closed form and whose step follows from
the field size; the second is a leave-one-out deconvolution whose direction rule and clamp deliver
every player’s coefficients from one product with an absolute error of O(nu). Both were tested on
1,511 exactly solvable instances with up to 4,000 players, stack ratios up to 109 and a wide range of
prize structures, and the errors stayed at the rounding floor throughout.
```
